he will sack, and the Germans who dwell on the furthest barbarian reaches of the Rhine,
and the arrow-shooting Iberians.
Straightway there will be another greatest evil for the Jews,
and Phoenicia beside them will drink showering blood;
and the walls of the Assyrians will fall before many warriors.
And again a life-destroying man will annihilate them.
And then there will be threats from the sovereign God,
earthquakes and great famines throughout all the earth,
and unseasonable snowstorms, and moreover fierce thunderbolts.
And then indeed the great king, amid the turmoil of Ares,
a mountain-roaming Celt hastening into the strife of battle,
will not escape an unseemly fate, but will perish;
a foreign dust will conceal him as a corpse, and he shall have a name
bearing the name of a flower. And after him another will rule,
a silver-headed man, whose name will be that of a sea,
bearing the initial letter, a four-syllable Ares.
He will also dedicate temples in all the cities,
inspecting the world on his own foot, bringing gifts,
and he will supply much gold and amber to many.
He will also grasp all the mysteries of magic arts
from the shrines; and indeed far better for humankind
he will establish as ruler . . . thunderbolt;
and there will be a long peace, when this man
is sovereign; and he will also be a sweet-voiced singer
and a participant in laws, an upright dispenser of justice;
and he himself will fall in turn, coming to his end by his own fate.
After him three will rule, but the third will hold sway late,
holding three decades; but again from the first unit
another king will rule; and after him another sovereign
from seven decades; their names will be noble.
And they in turn will destroy tattooed peoples,
Britons, Moors, great Dacians, and Arabs.
But whenever the youngest of these shall perish,
then dreadful Ares will once again advance against Parthia,
the one who wounded it before, and will utterly ravage it.
And then the king himself will fall beneath a treacherous beast,
exercising his hands; and this will be the pretext for his death.
After him another man will rule, knowing many wise things,
having the name ... of the first mighty king
from the first unit; and he will be both good and great;
and many things will he mightily accomplish for the great Latins
for the sake of his father's memory; straightway the walls of Rome
he will adorn with gold, silver, and ivory,
going into forums and temples with mighty light.
And at some time a most terrible wound will shoot up in wars
for the Romans; and he will sack the whole land
of the Germans, when a great sign from God
appears from heaven, and saves bronze-helmeted men
who are exhausted, because of the king's piety;
for the heavenly God will completely heed him,
and when he prays, will rain down timely shower-water.
But whenever these things which I have spoken are fulfilled,
then indeed the renowned reign of the great, pious king
will fail as the years roll round;
and at the end of his life, having openly designated his own offspring
as he enters upon the royal palace, he will die by his own destiny,
leaving the royal rule to a blond-haired sovereign,
who will have the name of two decades; having become king
from his father by birth, he will succeed to the rule.
This man will hold everything with excessive calculation;
he will zealously imitate high-spirited, overbearing Heracles
and will excel in mighty arms,
having the greatest renown in hunts and horsemanship;
yet he will live dangerously, all alone.
And there will be a fearful sign while this man rules:
upon the soil of Rome there will be a cloud and a mist,
so that no mortal can see the one next to him.
And then indeed wars and grievous troubles will come together,
when the king himself, mad with lust, raging,
will come, disgracing his own family in the bedchamber,
shameful in unadvised and unholy marriages.
Then indeed a great, destructive man, hidden in bereavement,
harboring wrath, will heap up evils in a bathhouse,
a murderous man bound by treacherous fates.
Know then that Rome's destructive time is near
because of rivalry for the sovereignty; and many will perish
in the halls of Pallas by the hands of Ares.
And then Rome will be widowed and will pay in full for all things,
as much as she alone did formerly in many wars.
My heart weeps, and my soul within me weeps;
for from the time when the first king, O haughty Rome,
established one good law for earthly mortals,
[and the Word of the great immortal God came to earth,]
until the end of the nineteenth kingship,
a time of twice one hundred, twice twenty, and twice two years,
in addition to six months, should be fulfilled; then the race—
widowed, the twentieth king, when in your halls
he pours out blood by the sword, struck by sharp bronze,
having the letter that signifies the number eighty
as a name, and having heavy old age; and he will make it widowed
in a short time, when many warriors,
and many falls and slaughters and slayings of men,
and destructive strifes and miseries for the sake of victory
in sovereign rule, and many horses and men mingled together
will fall upon the ground, slaughtered in wars.
And then another man will come, having the sign of the tenth number
of a name, and he will cause many
griefs and groans, and indeed he will lay waste many;
but he himself in turn will be short-lived and will fall,
struck down in mighty Ares by flashing iron.
Another warrior will come of the number fifty,
raised up from the East for the sake of sovereignty;
and warlike Ares will advance as far even as Thrace;
and he will flee thereafter and come to the plain of the Bithynians
and the soil of the Cilicians; but swiftly brazen Ares,
soul-destroying, will lay him waste on the Assyrian plains.
And then, knowing deceitful means to gain power,
a man of cunning counsel raised up from the West,
will have a name with the sign of the number two hundred;
far more for the sake of royal rule
he will stir up war, against the Assyrian people
having gathered his whole army, and will subject all things.
And great power will rule the Romans; and in his mind
is much contrivance, the wrath of destructive Ares;
a dread serpent and grievous in war, who will destroy all
earthly mortals that are born high and noble,
and having slain noble men for the sake of wealth, like a star,
having plundered the whole land of perishing men—
he will march toward the East; and every deceit will be theirs.
Then, when a child Caesar reigns with him,
bearing the name of the mighty Macedonian king
from the initial letter; and having driven off the strife around him,
he will escape the sheer deceit of the approaching king
in the bosom of the army; but he, with barbarian customs
ruling suddenly, the temple-keeper, will perish,
subdued in mighty Ares by flashing iron;
Him, even when dead, the people will mutilate.
And then indeed the kings of the Persians will rise up
... Roman Ares ... the Roman king.
And Phrygia, rich in flocks, will groan with earthquakes.
Alas, Laodicea; alas, wretched Hierapolis;
for you were the first that the yawning earth once swallowed up.
... monstrous ... Aus[onia] ...
all things that ...
will wail ... of perishing men
in the hands of Ares; and an evil fate will be yours
among men; but then also along the way from the East,
hastening to look upon Italy, with flashing iron
stripped bare, he will fall, having aroused hatred because of his mother.
For the seasons ... all ... and [the four]th will hold another
of the burning ... but not all know this at once;
for not all things belong to all; but only those will have delight
who will serve God and have forgotten idols.
And now, Lord of the cosmos, King of every kingdom,
infallible, immortal one—for you have placed in my heart
an ambrosial voice—bring my speech to an end; for indeed I do not know
what things I say; for you are the one within me who declares all things.
Give me a brief rest, and put a lovely song
into my heart; for the heart within me has grown weary
of divinely inspired verses, prophesying royal dominions.
Thirteenth Oracle of the Sibyl
... commands me to sing a great word [concerning] God,
the holy, immortal, imperishable God, who to kings
gave power and took it away, and appointed a time for them
of both: of life and of destructive death.
And these things the heavenly God urges me, unwilling,
to announce to kings concerning royal dominion.
And the spear of furious Ares; and by him all will perish.
And having become a child-ruler, he gives decrees in assemblies;
for many wars, battles, and slaughters of men,
famines, plagues, earthquakes, and fierce thunderbolts,
and many incursions of the Assyrians throughout the whole world,
as well as pillaging and the plundering of temples.
And then indeed will be the uprising of the enterprising Persians,
and of Indians, Armenians, and Arabs together; and against them
the Roman king, insatiable of war, will approach,
leading spearmen against the Assyrians as well, a young Ares;
even unto the deep-flowing, silver-swirling Euphrates
warlike Ares will advance, sending his spear,
for the sake of ...; for indeed, betrayed by a comrade,
he will fall in battle, struck down by flashing iron.
And immediately again a lover of purple and a warrior,
appearing from Syria, a terror of Ares, will rule together with his son
as Caesar, and will ravage every land; and the name for them
is one for both: upon the twenty-first [letter]
five hundreds are set. And when these...
they shall rule in wars, and when they become lawgivers,
there shall be a brief cessation of war, not for long;
but when a wolf pledges oaths of trust for a flock
before sharp-toothed hounds, and then does harm,
injuring the woolly sheep, and casts aside the oaths;
even then an unlawful strife of arrogant kings
shall arise in wars, and Syrians shall perish terribly,
along with Indians, Armenians, Arabs, Persians, and Babylonians.
They shall destroy one another through mighty battles.
But when Roman Ares destroys the German,
having conquered the heart-destroying Ares of the Ocean,
truly then for the Persians also, arrogant men,
there shall be a war of many years, but victory shall not be theirs;
for as on a lofty, many-ridged, wind-swept,
steep cliff a fish does not swim upon the summit,
nor does a tortoise fly, nor does an eagle swim into the water,
so too are the Persians far removed from victory
on that day, for as long as the dear nurse of Italians,
lying in the plain beside the divine water of the Nile,
sends the portion of the harvest to seven-hilled Rome.
And these things are fated: for as great a number as your name, O Rome, contains in the reckoning of calculated time,
for so many years willingly shall she measure out grain for you,
the noble, great city of the Macedonian king.
And another grievous woe shall I sing for the Alexandrians,
who perish on account of the strife of disgraceful men.
Men who were formerly cowardly and weak
shall welcome peace because of the wickedness of their leaders.
And wrath from the great God shall come upon the Assyrians,
and a torrent of a river shall destroy them, which coming
into the cities of Caesar shall harm the Canaanites.
Pyramus shall irrigate the city of Mopsus, where
Aegeans shall fall through the strife of exceedingly violent men.
Wretched Antioch, grievous Ares shall not leave you,
when the Assyrian war presses hard around you;
for in your palaces shall dwell a champion of men,
who shall war against all the arrow-shooting Persians,
himself being born of the royal realm of the Romans.
Now adorn yourselves, cities of the Arabs, with temples and stadiums
and broad marketplaces and splendidly shining wealth,
and with images of gold, silver, and ivory;
and above all, though you are devoted to astrology,
Bostra and Philippopolis, that you may enter into great mourning;
for the exulting spheres of the zodiacal circle
shall not profit you—Aries, Taurus, and Gemini—
nor all the hour-watching stars that appear
with them in the sky, O wretched one, in which you greatly trust,
whenever that appointed day of yours approaches from behind.
And now I will sing for the war-loving Alexandrians
most terrible wars; and indeed a great multitude of people shall perish,
citizens being destroyed by rival townsmen.
as they contend for the sake of hateful strife; and around them
grim-visaged Ares, rushing on, will make war to cease.
And then again the great-hearted one, together with his mighty son,
shall fall treacherously on account of an elder king.
And after him in turn shall rule over mighty, flourishing Rome
another great-hearted king, skilled in waging war,
rising up from the Dacians, of the number three hundred;
he shall be from the fourth horn, and he will destroy many,
and then indeed all brothers and friends
the king will destroy, and when the kings have perished,
straightway again there will be plunderings and murders of the faithful
suddenly, on account of the former king.
Then, whenever a crafty man comes upon the couch,
a bandit appearing out of Syria, an obscure Roman,
and he will approach treacherously the race of the Cappadocian men
and having besieged them, will fall upon them, insatiable for war,
then indeed for you, Tyana and Mazaca, there shall be capture;
you will be enslaved, and will place your neck under this man's yoke;
and Syria will lament for the people who are perishing,
nor will Selene then rescue the sacred city.
When from Syria one arrives first, fleeing outrageous insolence,
escaping the Romans across the streams of the Euphrates,
no longer resembling Romans, but the lordly,
arrow-shooting Persians, then the ruler of the Italians
shall fall in battle, struck down by gleaming iron,
leaving his realm; and in addition to him, his sons will perish.
But whenever another king rules over Rome,
and then unsettled nations come against the Romans,
baneful Ares with a bastard son against the walls of Rome, and then indeed famines, plagues, and fierce thunderbolts,
and terrible wars and tumults of cities
shall come suddenly; and the Syrians will perish terribly;
for upon them will come the great wrath of the Most High,
and straightway an uprising of the enterprising Persians,
and the Syrians, having mingled with the Persians, will destroy the Romans;
yet they shall not conquer, by the God-ordained purpose.
Ah, how many born of the East shall flee
with their possessions to foreign-speaking peoples!
Ah, the dark blood of how many men the earth will drink!
For that time will come in which the living,
pronouncing a blessing with their mouths upon those who have died,
will declare, 'It is good to die,' and death will flee from them.
And now for you, wretched Syria, I lament piteously;
a stroke will also come upon you from the arrow-shooting men,
a terrible one, which you never expected would come upon you.
There will also come the fugitive of Rome, lifting a great spear,
crossing the Euphrates together with many myriads,
who will burn you down and ill dispose all things.
Wretched Antioch, you they will never call a city,
whenever through your own folly you fall beneath the spears;
and having plundered all things and stripped you bare, he will abandon you
roofless, uninhabited; and suddenly someone beholding you will weep.
And you shall be a triumph, Hierapolis, and you, Beroea;
weep together with Chalcis over newly wounded children.
Alas, as many as dwell by steep Mount Casius,
and as many as dwell along Amanus, and as many as the Lycus washes,
and as many as Marsyas and silver-eddying Pyramus wash;
for even unto the borders of Asia they shall lay down spoils,
stripping the cities, and they will take away the images of all things,
and cast temples down upon the all-nourishing earth.
And at some time a great calamity will come upon Gaul and Pannonia,
and upon the Mysians and Bithynians, when a warrior shall arrive.
O Lycians, Lycians, a wolf comes to lap up blood,
when the Sanni come with city-sacking Ares,
and the Carpi draw near to fight against the Ausonians.
And then indeed a bastard son, through his shameless daring,
shall destroy the king, and immediately he himself shall perish
because of his impiety; and afterward another again shall rule,
bearing the rule by names; but quickly he in turn shall fall,
struck in mighty Ares by flashing iron.
And again the world will be disordered, while mortals perish
by plague and war. And the Persians to the toil of Ares
shall rush forth again, raging against the Ausonians.
And then there shall be flight of the Romans; but afterward
a priest shall come, the very last, sent by the sun,
appearing from Syria, and he shall accomplish everything by craft.
And then there shall be a city of the sun; and around it
the Persians will endure the fearful threats of the Phoenicians.
When again two warlike men shall rule as lords over the mighty Romans, one of whom shall hold
the number seventy, and the other the number of the third;
and then a high-necked bull, digging into the earth with his hooves
and raising dust with his two horns,
shall do many evils to a dark-skinned crawling serpent
dragging its trail with scales; and thereupon he himself will perish.
And after him another fair-horned stag will come,
hungering along the mountains, eager to feed in his belly on
venom-shooting beasts; then shall come, sent by the sun,
a terrible and fearsome lion, breathing out much flame.
Then indeed he in turn shall destroy with great and shameless daring
both the swift, well-horned stag and the greatest beast,
venom-shooting, fearsome, emitting many hissings,
and the sideways-walking goat; and glory attends him.
He himself, whole, uninjured, and unapproachable,
shall rule the Romans, and the Persians shall be powerless.
But, O Lord, King of the cosmos, O God, bring to an end the song
of our verses, and grant a lovely song.
Fourteenth Oracle of the Sibyl
Mankind, why in vain, as though you were immortal
and holding brief sway, do you think exceedingly high thoughts,
and all desiring to reign over mortals,
not perceiving that God himself [hates] the lust for rule,
he hates, and especially insatiably gluttonous kings,
dreadful and impious, and he rouses gloom upon them;
because instead of good deeds and righteous thoughts
they all preferred purple mantles and cloaks,
longing for wars, miseries, and slaughter.
The imperishable God dwelling in the ether will make them short-lived,
utterly destroying them, and he will destroy one here and another there.
But whenever the slayer of bulls comes, trusting in his might,
fair-haired and grim, and destroys them all
and crushes the shepherds, and there will be no strength in them,
unless indeed by swiftness of foot the hounds through the glens
shall meet for strife, eager to pursue;
and the hound pursued the lion that was destroying the shepherds.
And then there will be a four-syllabled king, trusting in his might,
revealed from the initial letter; but quickly brazen Ares
will destroy him through the strife of insatiably gluttonous men.
Afterward two other men will rule as kings,
both of the number forty; and under them a great
peace of the world will come to all the people,
and ordinance and justice; but in turn men with flashing helmets,
in need of gold and silver, for the sake of this
will impiously kill them, seizing them with their hands.
And then again a dread young warrior will rule,
a ruler of the number seventy, destructive of soul, fiery,
who will impiously deliver the people of Rome to an army
to be slain in wickedness through the wrath of kings,
having laid low the whole glorious city of the Latins.
And Rome can no longer be seen, nor heard of,
such as a wayfarer saw her previously;
for all these things will lie in ashes, nor of the works
will there be any sparing; for he himself in his entirety will come
from heaven; firewinds from the ether and thunderbolts
the immortal God will send upon men; some he will destroy
with blazing lightning bolts, and others with chilling thunderbolts.
And then indeed they will kill the shameless, terrible ruler,
the childish Latins of mighty Rome.
Truly no light dust will lie upon him when dead,
but he will be sport for dogs and birds and wolves,
because he destroyed a martial people.
After him another famous ruler of the number forty will reign,
destroyer of Parthians, destroyer of Germans, having subdued the wild beasts,
dreadful and man-slaying, who by the streams of the ocean
and of the Euphrates continuously hold sway.
And then indeed Rome will again be as it was before.
But when a great wolf comes into his plains,
the ruler having arrived from the west will afterward die,
slain by strong Ares with sharp bronze.
And then again another great-hearted Ares, revealed from Assyria, will rule over the mighty Romans,
of the initial letter, and by wars he will subject all things;
he himself together with his armies will display his dominion,
And he will establish laws; but soon brazen Ares
will destroy him, fallen among treacherous armies.
After him three will rule, possessing an arrogant heart,
one having the number of a unit, and one of three tens,
and another sovereign will share in three hundred.
Wretched ones, who in much fire will melt down
gold and silver, the foundations of handmade temples,
and arming for victory, they will give money
to armies, distributing many fine treasures;
and eager for shameful deeds, they will likewise ravage
the arrow-shooting Parthians of deep-flowing Euphrates,
and hostile Medes, and soft-haired warriors,
Massagetae and Persians, quiver-bearing men.
But when the king comes to an end by his own fate,
leaving the royal sceptre to his younger sons
and enjoining justice, they straightway forgetting
their father's commands and arming their hands for Ares,
will rush into strife for the royal rule.
And then a sole ruler again, another from the third,
will reign, and will quickly meet his fate, struck down by a spear.
After him, many mighty mortals thereafter will perish
at one another's hands for the royal rule.
And one great-hearted elder ruler of the fourth
of the mighty Romans will rule, and will arrange all things well.
And then there will be war and strife in Phoenicia,
when the nations of arrow-shooting Persians come near.
Alas, how many will fall before barbarous-tongued men!
Sidon and Tripolis and boastful Berytus
will see one another in blood and corpses.
Wretched Laodicea, around her you raise up a great,
ineffectual war because of the impieties of men.
Alas, miserable Tyrians, you will reap the evil harvest,
when the sun that brings light to mortals fails in daytime,
and the disk appears not, and dense, frequent drops
of blood come down upon the earth from heaven.
And then indeed the king will die, betrayed by his companions.
And after him many shameless leaders
will kill one another, stirring up evil strife.
And then again there will be a venerable, wily lord,
numbering five in his name, trusting in great armies,
whom mortals will love for the sake of his royal rule;
and having a noble name, he will match it with noble deeds.
And there will be a fearful sign for you: while he is ruling,
between Taurus and snow-beaten Amanus,
a certain city of the Cilicians' land will perish utterly,
fair and strong, beside a mighty river.
And many earthquakes will occur in Propontis and the Phrygias;
and the renowned king by his own fate
will lose his life by a wasting sickness of death.
After him two royal lords will rule,
the one bearing the number of three hundred, and the other of three;
wherefore he shall destroy many on behalf of the city
of seven-hilled Rome, on account of his mighty rule.
And then evil shall come upon the senate, nor shall it escape
the king when he is enraged and harbours wrath against it.
There shall be a sign among all mortal men upon earth:
more frequent rains and snowfalls shall occur, and hail
shall destroy the fruits of the crops over the boundless earth.
And they themselves again shall fall, overcome in wars
by mighty Ares, for the sake of the Italians' war.
And then again another king of many wiles shall rule,
having gathered all the army and distributed wealth
to the bronze-armoured warriors for the sake of war; but thereafter
the Nile beyond grain-abundant Libya across the mainland
shall water the dark soil of Egypt for two years
and the arable land; but famine shall seize all things,
and war, and bandits, and slaughters, and manslaughters.
And many cities again, beneath warrior men,
shall perish by being overthrown by the hands of an army;
and he himself shall fall in turn, betrayed to flashing iron.
After him, one who obtained as his lot the number of three hundred
shall rule over the Romans and over haughty men;
he shall stretch out a soul-destroying spear against the Armenians,
the Parthians, the Assyrians, and the steadfast-in-battle Persians.
And then again there shall be a rebuilding of splendid Rome,
magnified in its ornament with gold, electrum,
silver, and ivory; and a vast populace in it,
from all the east and wealthy west,
shall dwell; and the king shall enact other laws for it;
and after this, upon a boundless island,
destructive death and mighty fate shall receive him.
And another man, of ten triads, like unto a beast
with flowing mane and grim countenance, shall rule, who shall be of Greek descent.
And then indeed the much-nourishing city of Phthia, the Molossians,
and famous Larissa and on the brows of the Peneus—
and then there shall be an uprising of horse-grazing Scythia.
And a terrible war by the waters of Lake Maeotis
shall take place, at the outflows beside the furthest mouth of the stream
of the water-crested Phasis, along the asphodel meadow;
many indeed shall fall at the hands of mighty warriors.
Ah, wretched ones, how many Ares shall receive with bronze!
And then indeed the king, having sacked the Scythian race,
shall die, releasing his life by his own appointed fate.
And another man, proclaimed after the four, shall rule in turn,
a dread man, whom all those who drink the thickest
ice of the strongly flowing Araxes, the Armenians,
shall dread in war, as well as the great-hearted Persians.
Between the Colchians and the very strong Pelasgians
there shall be dread wars and slaughters of men.
And the Phrygian land and the cities of the land of Propontis
And unsheathing two-edged swords from their scabbards,
they will strike one another down because of grievous impieties.
And then God will show a great sign to mortal humans
from heaven as the years revolve,
a sickle, a portent of an evil war to come.
And then the king will not escape the hands of the army,
but will die, subdued by hand with flashing iron.
After him another numbering fifty will rule in turn,
appearing from Asia, a terrible dread, a close-quarters fighter;
and he will wage war even against the glorious walls of Rome,
and against the Colchians, the Heniochoi, and the milk-drinking Agathyrsoi,
by the Euxine Sea and the sandy gulf of Thrace.
And then the king will not escape the hands of the army,
and even when he is a dead corpse they will mutilate him;
and then, when the king has perished, desolate will be
man-honoring Rome, and many people will perish.
And then in turn there will rule from greatest Egypt
one terrible and formidable, and he will destroy the great-hearted Parthians,
the Medes, the Germans, the Bosporans, and the Agathyrsoi,
the Britons, the Permanians, and the quiver-bearing Iberians,
the crooked Massagetae, and the overbearing Persians.
And then a glorious man will look upon all Greece,
hating Scythia and windy Caucasus.
And there will be a mighty sign for you; while he holds sway,
crowns from heaven from both south and north
will rise up, exactly resembling appearing stars.
And then he will leave the royal rule to his son,
for he begins with the initial letter, when by his own destiny
the manly king shall go into the halls of Hades.
But when this man's son rules in the land of Rome,
manifest from the unit, there will be throughout the whole earth
a great, much-desired peace; and him the Latins
will cherish as king on account of the honor of his father;
and though he hastens to go to both the East and the West,
the Romans will keep him, even against his will, at home,
ruling Rome, because indeed a friendly affection
was in all hearts toward the highly renowned sovereign king.
Yet destructive death will snatch him away after a short span of life,
betrayed by his own destiny.
And then again other mighty warriors
will strike one another down, putting forward evil strife,
possessing not a royal palace, but one of tyrants.
And they will indeed accomplish many evils in the whole world,
and especially for the Romans, until the third Dionysus,
until Ares helmet-clad comes from Egypt,
whom they call lord Dionysus by surname.
But whenever a murderous lion and a murderous lioness
tear the glorious purple royal garment,
they will seize it with gasping breath as the kingdom is hard-pressed;
and then a holy ruler, who has obtained the initial letter,
having contended with hostile leaders for victory,
he will cast them off to be food for dogs and birds of prey.
Alas for you, city burned with fire, mighty Rome,
how much you must suffer when all these things come to pass!
Yet afterward a great and renowned king
with gold and amber, silver and ivory,
will rebuild you completely, and in the world you will surpass all
in possessions, temples, market-places, riches, and stadiums;
and then you will once again be a light to all, even as you were before.
Alas, wretched Cecropians, Cadmeans, and Lakonians,
who dwell around the Peneus and deep-rushed Molossis,
Trikke, Dodona, and high-built Ithome,
and the Pierian ridge around the great peak of Olympus,
Ossa, Larissa, and high-gated Calydon.
But when God works a great sign for mortal men,
a daytime darkened like the dead of night across the world,
even then your end will come, O king, nor could you escape
the sharp bow of your brother aimed at you.
And then again there will rule a soul-destroying, boundless, fiery man,
sprung from the lineage of a king, who will have his descent from Egypt,
younger indeed, but far better than his brother,
who received the stamped sign of rule numbering eighty.
And then the heart-grieving wrath of the immortal God
the whole world will receive into its bosom because of pride;
for there will come upon mortal, short-lived men
famines, plagues, wars, and slaughters of men,
and relentless darkness upon the earth, the mother of peoples,
and confusion of the seasons, and unyielding wrath
from heaven, earthquakes and blazing thunderbolts,
and showers of stones and parched drizzles.
And the steep peaks of the Phrygian land were shaken,
the roots of the Scythian mountains shook, cities trembled,
and the whole earth trembled among them, as well as the land of Hellas.
And many cities, when God is greatly angered,
will fall headlong under smoking thunderbolts
and lamentations, and it will not be possible to flee nor escape his wrath.
And then again a king will fall by the hand of the army,
struck down by his own men as no one ever was.
After him, many Latin men will rise up again,
men clothed with purple mantles upon their shoulders,
who will desire by lot to seize royal rule.
And then three kings over the splendid walls of Rome
will arise, two holding the first number,
and one bearing strife as his surname as no one else;
they will love Rome and the whole world,
caring for mortal men; but they will achieve no success,
for God is not propitious to the world, nor will he be
gentle toward men, because they have wrought many evil deeds.
Therefore he will bring upon the kings an unseemly fury,
far worse than that of panthers and wolves; for them unsparingly...
the bronze-corsleted men taking them with their own hands,
subdued without resistance, cowardly as women,
shall destroy the kings upon their own sceptres.
Alas, wretched eminent men of glorious Rome,
persuaded by deceitful oaths you shall utterly perish.
And then indeed many spear-bearing rulers, in disorderly fashion,
men rushing on, shall take away generations
with the blood of first-born men . . .
twice such a pitiable fate does God then bring, and not for the first time,
and he will destroy all people by their own deeds.
Yet again God will bring those who have a shameless heart
to come into judgment, as many as devised evils;
they themselves shall devise plans, setting upon one another,
longing for this very internal judgment of wickedness.
{All the stars shall fall prow-to-prow into the sea,}
many stars in succession, and a beaming comet,
{a star which mortals call a portent of distress,}
of much distress coming on, of war and battle. —
And when again he gathers many oracles concerning the islands,
foretelling battle and slaughter to foreigners
and grievous ruin to the holy place, he shall quickly command
to gather wheat and barley into the dwellings of Rome, hastening after wealth for twelve months.
And the city shall be wretched in those days,
yet immediately it shall be prosperous again, and not in small measure;
and there shall be peace, whenever the ruling power perishes.
And then a final one reigning over the race of the Latins
shall be, and after it a kingdom shall spring up,
children and the race of children shall remain unshaken;
for it shall be known to him, since God himself reigns.
There is a certain land, a dear nurse to humankind,
lying in a plain, and around it the Nile bounds,
wafting prosperous winds over all Libya and Ethiopia,
and Syrians, transient men from various quarters, plunder
all the equipment from this land; where there shall be a great
and trusty lord, a king of children and sending to men.
And planning terrible things concerning the most terrible matters of all,
a strong helper to those of all proud Italy;
and when he comes unto the wine-dark sea of Assyria
and lays waste the Phoenicians in their homes,
binding on evil war and dread strife,
there shall be one ruler of the two realms of the earth.
And now I will sing the toil-filled end for the Alexandrians:
barbarians shall inhabit holy Egypt,
unharmed and unshaken, whenever envy comes from somewhere;
{but when God changes the seasons . . .}
making winter into summer, then all the divine decrees are accomplished.
But whenever three youths win the Olympic games,
and even if they declare the divinely heard oracles,
and first purify with the blood of a suckling quadruped,
then three times may the Most High bring a dreadful fate,
Whenever he stretches out his mournful long spear against all,
then much barbarian blood shall flow in the dust,
when the city is sacked by inhospitable strangers.
Blessed is he who has died, and blessed is whoever is childless;
for under a slavish yoke he shall place his neck,
he who formerly exercised leadership renowned for freedom,
he who previously rolled out famous counsels;
such multifaceted slavery will the ruler impose.
And then immediately an ill-fated army of Sicilians will arrive,
bringing terror, whenever a vast barbarian nation advances;
when they produce fruit, they will divide the plowed fields.
To them the high-thundering God will give evil instead of good;
stranger will constantly plunder hateful gold from stranger.
But when all behold the blood of the raw-devouring
lion, and a murderous lioness comes upon the body
from off his head, and casts the scepter away from him,
then as when all the peoples in Egypt partake
in a beloved feast, and accomplish mighty deeds,
and one restrains another, while a great battle-cry is among them—
even so will terror fall upon men
from raging strife, and many others shall perish,
killing one another in harsh battle.
And then one clad in dark-blue scales will come;
two others will come together in unison,
and with them a third, a great ram from Cyrene,
whom I previously spoke of fleeing battle beside the streams of the Nile;
yet even so, they shall all accomplish an unavailing course.
And then, as great years roll around,
there will be long spans of deep quiet; but thereafter
a second war will again be set among them in Egypt,
and there will be a naval battle, but there will be no victory for them.
O wretched ones, there will be the defeat of a distinguished city,
and it will become a spoil of wars, though not for long.
And then indeed men bordering a vast land
will flee in cowardice, and lead away their gray-haired parents.
And again, possessing great victory, they will encounter the youth;
they will destroy the Judeans, steadfast warriors,
plundering in wars as far as the gray sea,
both being shepherds, fighting for fatherland and parents.
And he will assign the race of trophy-bearing men among the dead.
Alas, how many men will swim around the waves!
For many will lie upon the sandy shores;
fair heads will fall prey to Egyptian birds;
then indeed mortal blood will pursue the Arabs.
But whenever wolves again confirm pledges of trust with dogs
on a sea-girt island, then there will be a raising up of towers,
and men will inhabit the city that suffered much.
For no longer will there be deceitful gold nor silver,
no possession of land, no toilsome slavery;
but one friendship and one way of life for a glad-hearted people.
All things will be common, and there will be one equal light of life.
Evil in the earth will plunge into the divine sea.
And then the harvest of mortal humankind was near at hand.
A strong necessity lies upon these things to be accomplished.
No other wayfarer meeting another will then say,
that the race of perishing mortals will ever cease.
And then the holy nation will hold the scepters of all the earth
unto all ages together with their noble progenitors.
Mortal and fleshly humans, who are nothing,
how quickly are you exalted, not looking toward the end of life?
Do you not tremble nor fear God, your overseer,
the Most High, the all-knowing, the all-seeing witness of all things,
the all-nourishing Creator, who placed His sweet breath in all,
and made it a guide for all mortals?
There is one God, who alone rules, exceedingly great, unbegotten,
Almighty, invisible, Himself beholding all things,
yet Himself unseen by any mortal flesh.
For what flesh is able to look upon the heavenly and true,
immortal God with eyes, He who inhabits the vault of heaven?
For not even against the rays of the sun
are humans able to stand, being mortal-born
men, being veins and flesh upon bones.
Worship Him, the only existing ruler of the cosmos,
who alone exists unto eternity and from eternity,
self-begotten, unbegotten, holding power over all things through all time,
administering judgment to all mortals in the common light.
You shall receive the worthy reward of your evil counsel,
because you abandoned the true and eternal God
to glorify Him and sacrifice holy hecatombs to Him,
and instead offered your sacrifices to the demons in Hades.
You walk in delusion and madness, and having left
the upright, straight path, you departed and through thorns
and stakes you wander. Cease, vain mortals,
roaming in darkness and rayless, black night,
and leave the darkness of night, and lay hold of the light!
Behold, He is plain and unerring to all.
Come, do not continually pursue darkness and gloom!
Behold, the sweet-beholding light of the sun shines exceedingly.
Know this, having laid up wisdom in your breasts:
there is one God, who sends forth rains, winds, earthquakes,
lightnings, famines, plagues, and mournful sorrows,
and snowstorms and ice. Why indeed do I recount them one by one?
He rules heaven, He governs earth, He Himself exists.
If gods reproduce and remain immortal,
the gods who were born would have become more numerous than humans,
and there would never have been any place for mortals to stand.
If anything is generated at all, it also perishes; God cannot
be fashioned from the loins and womb of a man.
Rather, God alone is one, the all-supreme, who made
heaven and the sun and the stars and the moon.
the fruit-bearing earth and the swelling waves of the sea,
the lofty mountains and the ever-flowing streams of springs.
And again of aquatic creatures he generates a vast, innumerable host,
and creeping things moving on the earth are nourished with life,
and various kinds of birds, shrill-voiced, twittering,
nimble, with piercing wing-cries, stirring the air with their pinions;
and in the mountain glens he placed the wild breed of beasts,
and to us mortals he subjected all the cattle.
And as leader of all he established one fashioned by God,
and subjected to man things manifold and incomprehensible.
For what flesh of mortals is able to know all these things?
Nay, he alone knows, who made these things from the beginning,
the imperishable, eternal Creator who dwells in the ether,
offering to the good a good, far greater reward,
but against the wicked and the unrighteous stirring up wrath and fury,
and war and pestilence and tearful pains.
O humans, why are you vainly puffed up and uprooted?
Be ashamed, you who deify weasels and wild beasts!
Does not madness and frenzy take away the perception of your minds,
if gods steal dishes and plunder pots?
Instead of dwelling in the boundless, golden heaven,
they appear moth-eaten and are veiled with dense spiderwebs.
Worshiping serpents, dogs, and cats, senseless ones,
you even revere birds and creeping beasts of the earth,
and stone images and handmade idols,
and heaps of stones by the roadsides—these you revere,
and many other vain things, which it is indeed shameful even to mention.
These are gods, the treacherous guides of senseless mortals,
from whose mouth indeed deadly poison is poured out.
He who is both life and imperishable, everlasting light,
and pours forth for mortals a joy sweeter than honey...
...bend the neck to him alone,
and direct your path for all ages among the pious.
Leaving all these things, the cup full of judgment,
strong, weighty, heavily laden, exceedingly unmixed,
you have all drained in foolishness with a raving spirit.
And you do not wish to sober up and come to a sound mind,
and to know God the King, who watches over all.
Therefore the flash of burning fire is coming upon you;
you will be burned with torches throughout the age all day long,
put to shame for your false, useless idols.
But those who honor the true and everlasting God
inherit life, throughout all the duration of the age,
dwelling together in the luxuriant garden of Paradise,
feasting on sweet bread from the starry heaven.
Listen to me, mortals: the eternal King reigns.
He who alone is God, being the unconquerable Creator;
he himself established the form and figure of mortals,
he himself blended the nature of all things, the father of life.
Whenever he comes,
There will be fire in the midst of dark, black night.
[God is] uncreated.
The Erythraean, at any rate, [spoke] to God: 'Why indeed,' she says, 'O Master, do you
impose on me the necessity of prophecy, and not rather, lifted on high from the earth,
preserve me until the most blessed [occasion] of your coming
day?'
